<document>
# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
I checked the arithmetic, and it's internally consistent:
- Sector counts sum to 61 organisations and 2,940 employees.
- The employee-weighted output index works out to 98.73.
- Each per-hour figure is the index divided by 0.8.
- The percentage changes in Table 2 are correct.

The problem is the inferences. **The headline claims, especially "sector-general," go well beyond what the design and data support, and several results are partly produced by how they were measured.** The authors list most of the relevant limitations, then set them aside without engaging them.

## 1. The per-hour gain in every sector is guaranteed by the metric

Output per scheduled hour is the index divided by 0.8. Any organisation whose output fell by less than 20% therefore shows a per-hour gain.

- An organisation that lost 15% of its output would be reported as "+6% productivity."
- So "gains in output per hour in every sector" is close to a tautology, not a finding. The fact that it "held in retail" is not evidence, because it could hardly have failed to.

The more informative figure is the raw index, which the report plays down:
- **Overall output fell 1.3%.** The pilot's own principle was "100% of the output," so the target was narrowly missed, not met.
- **Retail and hospitality output fell 6.9%.** For low-margin, demand-driven businesses, that is a large loss.

## 2. The data cut against "sector-general"

| Sector | Organisations | Reverted | Share reverted |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 3 | **50%** |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 2 | **40%** |
| All other sectors | 50 | 0 | 0% |

- Every reversion came from the two sectors where output is most tied to staffed time. Those are also the two sectors with the lowest output indices.
- "Output per hour" is also the wrong lens for coverage-based work. If staggered days kept a shop open, sales depend on customer demand, not staff hours. The real cost then shows up as coverage, overtime or service quality, none of which were measured.

What the data actually suggest is close to the opposite of the conclusion: the model held up in office and knowledge work and showed clear strain in customer-facing sectors. That rests on 11 organisations, so it's suggestive at best, but it is the honest reading.

## 3. The primary outcome is the weakest measure in the study

The output index was:
- **Reported by the managers responsible for the pilot.**
- **Based on differing records** in each organisation.
- **Unblinded.**
- **Set against an explicit target of 100**, under a pilot framed as "100% of the output."

That is a recipe for numbers that cluster just below 100, which is what we see. The report lists this as Limitation 3, but it is not a side issue: it is the primary outcome. Every per-hour claim depends on it.

There is also a baseline inconsistency:
- **Revenue** is compared with the same months a year earlier, "to remove seasonality."
- **The output index** is compared with the six months immediately before the pilot, with no seasonal adjustment.

If seasonality matters enough to correct for in revenue, it matters for output too.

## 4. Revenue is weaker than presented

- A 1.4% nominal rise over 2023–24 is likely a fall in real terms, given inflation in most economies during that period.
- Nine of the 61 organisations (15%) didn't report revenue, and we aren't told which ones or why. If they were disproportionately from retail, the gap matters.
- Revenue isn't broken down by sector.

"No sign that output was sacrificed" is too strong. "Not clearly informative" is the fair description.

## 5. Sick days fall partly by construction

With four scheduled days a week instead of five, there are 20% fewer days on which anyone can take sick leave. On that basis alone, 4.4 days would fall to about 3.5.

- The actual figure is 2.8, so the like-for-like reduction is about **20%, not 36%**. That's still a real improvement, but the headline overstates it by roughly 16 points.
- Seasonality may also matter, depending on which months formed the baseline. Six months before the pilot likely includes winter.

## 6. Resignations and continuation are weak evidence

**Resignations:**
- Staff are unlikely to resign during a pilot that gives them an extra day off. That effect lasts only as long as the pilot.
- The 2023 labour market was also cooling.
- With no control group, a 56% drop over six months, annualised, can't be attributed to the pilot.

**Continuation:**
- The organisations volunteered and spent two months preparing.
- The decision to continue was made by the same managers who reported the output.
- Withdrawing a day off is costly for morale.
- Only 18 organisations made the change permanent. The other 38 "continuing" may include extended trials.

So "the high continuation rate is itself evidence" mainly reflects the organisations' commitment, not the model's effectiveness.

## 7. The wellbeing results show a fade the discussion ignores

Self-reported energy rose 0.61 SD at month three but only 0.29 SD at month six: **more than half the gain was gone within three months.** That pattern fits a novelty or Hawthorne effect. It also undercuts the "rested employees" explanation, which would predict a stable effect.

The report gives neither a survey response rate nor attrition between waves.

## 8. The causal story isn't tested

"Reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation" is asserted, not shown. Managers themselves described the cut in hours as a "forcing device" for:
- fewer and shorter meetings (47 of 58 managers),
- protected focus time,
- simpler approvals,
- dropping low-value reporting.

Any of these could be implemented without cutting hours. The design can't separate the two explanations, and the managers' own accounts point more toward process changes than toward fatigue.

## 9. Other gaps

- **Actual hours weren't measured.** If staff worked on their day off or lengthened their other days, the per-hour gain is overstated, possibly by a lot.
- **Nine organisations withdrew before the pilot began** and are excluded from all analysis. That is 13% of enrolment, filtered out before any outcome was measured.
- **No spread or uncertainty is reported.** There are only employee-weighted means: no distribution across organisations, no confidence intervals, no statistical tests. Weighting by employees also lets large knowledge-work organisations dominate the averages.
- **Self-selection** limits generalisation, which contradicts "sector-general" directly. The report concedes this in Limitation 1 and then draws the general conclusion anyway.

## 10. The dismissal of the limitations is circular

"Unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors." But:
- The **size** of the per-hour effect largely comes from dividing by 0.8.
- The **consistency** across sectors is guaranteed for any sector that lost less than 20% of its output.

Neither can be used to outweigh the limitations, because both are produced by the same unvalidated, manager-reported measure.

## What the evidence does support

Among self-selected organisations, mostly in office and knowledge work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay coincided with manager-reported output about 1% below baseline. Staff reported substantially better wellbeing, though part of that faded by month six. Customer-facing sectors showed larger output losses and a high reversion rate. Without a control group, independent output measures, or data on actual hours, the size of any productivity effect can't be estimated.

That is still a worthwhile and encouraging result for knowledge work. It simply isn't evidence that the model is sector-general, and the report's own retail data point the other way.

One connection to your first document: its section 4 example ("a trial shows a new form reduces errors at two sites… plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow") is essentially the inference this paper makes for retail and hospitality. The report even includes the evidence that the different-workflow case behaves differently.

If useful, I can draft a referee report in standard format, or suggest a stronger design for the follow-up pilot.
